lore.title: The Goddess of the Oil Village
lore.excerpt: Khokana is a traditional Newar village south of Patan, known for its mustard oil, pressed for generations in wooden presses, and for its well-preserved village life. At its centre stands the temple of Rudrayani, the village's protective goddess, one of the mot…

lore.title: A Village Pagoda
lore.excerpt: Rudrayani's temple is a pagoda in the Newar style, with brick walls, carved wooden struts and doors, and tiled roofs, standing in the village's central area. The temple is surrounded by traditional houses with carved windows, many of them damaged in 2015 and s…

lore.title: Rudrayani, Mother Protector
lore.excerpt: Rudrayani is understood as a form of the mother goddess associated with Rudra, a fierce form of Shiva, and she is honoured as the protector of Khokana and its people. In the Newar tradition, towns and villages are protected by a circle of mother goddesses, the…

lore.title: Shikali Jatra and Village Life
lore.excerpt: Khokana's most important festival is the Shikali Jatra, held in the autumn around the time of Dashain, when the village honours its goddesses with processions, masked dances, music and rituals over several days. The festival draws residents who have moved away…

lore.title: Rebuilding a Traditional Village
lore.excerpt: Khokana suffered heavy damage in the 2015 earthquake, with many traditional houses destroyed and others badly cracked, and the temple of Rudrayani was also affected. Reconstruction has been a long process involving the community, local authorities and heritage…

monuments.audioHook: Smell the air in Khokana and you may catch the sharp scent of mustard oil. For generations this village has pressed oil in heavy wooden presses, and some still work today. At the centre of the village stands the temple of Rudrayani, the mother goddess who protects Khokana. Every autumn, during the Shikali festival, vil…

monuments.talkingPoint: Introduce Khokana's goddess, its oil presses and its rebuilding.

lore.title: Ganesh Who Makes Things Happen
lore.excerpt: On a wooded hilltop between the villages of Bungamati and Khokana stands the shrine of Karya Binayak, a form of Ganesh whose name means 'the Ganesh who accomplishes tasks'. Karya Binayak is an important Ganesh shrine of the southern valley, and devotees come h…

lore.title: A Hilltop Shrine Among Trees
lore.excerpt: The shrine of Karya Binayak is modest in form, a small structure sheltering the natural stone image, surrounded by trees and smaller shrines on the hilltop. Its simplicity reflects the nature of the deity's manifestation: the holiness lies in the rock itself r…

lore.title: The Self-Manifested Ganesh
lore.excerpt: Ganesh, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati, is the remover of obstacles and the lord of beginnings, worshipped before any new undertaking. At Karya Binayak the god is manifested in a natural rock, svayambhu or self-arisen, rather than in a sculpted i…

lore.title: Prayers Before Undertakings
lore.excerpt: Devotees visit Karya Binayak to pray before beginning important tasks, offering flowers, rice, red powder, sweets and coins. Tuesdays, sacred to Ganesh in Nepal, bring additional worshippers, and Ganesh Chaturthi, the god's festival, is a major occasion. Stude…

lore.title: Protecting a Sacred Grove
lore.excerpt: Karya Binayak's hilltop setting, with its trees and shrines, is as important as the shrine itself, and protecting the woodland from encroachment and degradation is essential. The 2015 earthquake damaged buildings in Bungamati and Khokana, and the shrine and it…

monuments.audioHook: On a wooded hill between the villages of Bungamati and Khokana sits a small shrine with a big job. This is Karya Binayak, the Ganesh who makes things happen. The god here was not carved by any sculptor: he is a natural rock, smeared with red powder, believed to have revealed himself in stone. People climb up before exa…

monuments.talkingPoint: Explain the self-manifested Ganesh on the village walk to Bungamati.

lore.title: Home of the Rain God
lore.excerpt: Bungamati, a Newar village south of Patan, is considered the birthplace and second home of Rato Machhindranath, the 'Red Matsyendranath', worshipped by Newar Buddhists as Bunga Dyah or Karunamaya, the compassionate Avalokiteshvara, and by Hindus as Matsyendran…

lore.title: A Shikhara in a Village Square
lore.excerpt: Rato Machhindranath's temple at Bungamati is a shikhara, a tall tapering tower, standing in the centre of the village's main square. The square is surrounded by traditional Newar houses, rest houses and shrines, creating an ensemble that had changed little in …

lore.title: The Compassionate Red God
lore.excerpt: Rato Machhindranath's image is painted red, the colour associated with compassion and with the deity's role as giver of rain and fertility. For Newar Buddhists he is Karunamaya, 'full of compassion', a form of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, who vowed to save…

lore.title: The Longest Chariot Festival
lore.excerpt: Rato Machhindranath's chariot festival, held each spring before the monsoon, is the longest and one of the most important festivals in the Kathmandu Valley. A towering chariot, built anew each year from timber and bamboo following strict traditional rules, car…

lore.title: Rebuilding After 2015
lore.excerpt: The 2015 earthquake devastated Bungamati, destroying the Rato Machhindranath temple and many traditional houses. The collapse of the temple was a heavy blow to the community, and its reconstruction became a priority. Rebuilding has been carried out with the in…

monuments.audioHook: In the middle of this village square stands the temple of Rato Machhindranath, the red god of rain. Legend says a terrible drought once struck the valley because the yogi Gorakhnath was sitting in meditation on the rain serpents. So the king fetched Gorakhnath's own teacher, Matsyendranath, from distant Assam. When the…
monuments.nepaliSummary: बुंगमतीको रातो मछिन्द्रनाथ मन्दिर वर्षाका देवता करुणामयको घर हो; २०१५ को भूकम्पमा ढलेपछि यसको पुनर्निर्माण गरियो।
monuments.talkingPoint: Tell the drought legend and explain the twelve-year chariot journey.

lore.title: One of Nepal's Oldest Pagodas
lore.excerpt: Indreshwar Mahadev, in the town of Panauti south-east of the Kathmandu Valley, is often described as one of the oldest and largest pagoda temples in Nepal, traditionally dated to 1294. The temple is dedicated to Shiva as Indreshwar, 'lord of Indra', a name lin…

lore.title: Struts from the Early Malla Age
lore.excerpt: Indreshwar Mahadev is a large three-tiered pagoda raised on a plinth, standing in a spacious courtyard surrounded by smaller shrines and buildings. Its roof struts are celebrated as some of the oldest surviving examples of Newar woodcarving, depicting deities …

lore.title: Indra's Penance
lore.excerpt: The legend of Indreshwar tells that Indra, king of the gods, came to this place to perform penance after committing an offence, and that Shiva, pleased with his devotion, granted him forgiveness and manifested here as a lingam. The temple's name honours this s…

lore.title: Panauti Jatra and Makar Mela
lore.excerpt: Panauti's festival calendar centres on the Panauti Jatra, a chariot festival held each year in late spring, when the town's deities, including Indreshwar Mahadev and the goddess Brahmayani, are carried in chariots through the streets. The festival is one of th…

lore.title: Restoring Panauti's Treasure
lore.excerpt: Indreshwar Mahadev has been repaired many times over its long history, including after the earthquake of 1988, which damaged temples in the region, and after the 2015 earthquake. Restoration work has involved national heritage authorities and international par…

monuments.audioHook: Panauti is a small town about thirty kilometres from Kathmandu, and at its heart stands one of the oldest pagoda temples in Nepal: Indreshwar Mahadev, traditionally dated to 1294. Look up at the roof struts. They are among the oldest surviving Newar woodcarvings anywhere, made long before the famous temples of the Durb…

lore.title: Panauti's Protective Goddess
lore.excerpt: Brahmayani is the tutelary goddess of Panauti, and her temple stands near the confluence of the rivers that make the town sacred. She is one of the Ashta Matrika, the eight mother goddesses who protect Newar towns, and is associated with Brahma, the creator go…

lore.title: A Riverside Temple
lore.excerpt: Brahmayani's temple is a Newar pagoda with brick walls, carved struts and tiled roofs, set near the riverbank where the Punyamati and Roshi rivers meet. Its riverside setting connects it with the ghats and with the rituals of bathing and purification performed…

lore.title: The Mother on a Swan
lore.excerpt: Brahmayani, also called Brahmani, is the shakti or female energy of Brahma, and she is often depicted riding a swan, Brahma's vehicle, and holding attributes associated with him, such as a water pot and a rosary. As one of the Ashta Matrika, she is part of the…

lore.title: The Goddess's Chariot
lore.excerpt: During the Panauti Jatra, held each year in late spring, Brahmayani's image is placed on a chariot and pulled through the streets of Panauti along with the chariots of other deities, including Indreshwar Mahadev. The festival lasts several days and includes ri…

lore.title: Rivers, Floods and Earthquakes
lore.excerpt: Brahmayani's riverside location exposes it to flooding during the monsoon, as well as to the earthquakes that have affected Panauti over the centuries. The 1988 and 2015 earthquakes damaged temples in the area, and repairs were carried out by local authorities…

monuments.audioHook: Cross toward the river in Panauti and you reach the temple of Brahmayani, the mother goddess who protects this town. Look for her vehicle, a swan, borrowed from Brahma the creator, whose female power she embodies. Her temple stands near the confluence where two visible rivers and, tradition says, one invisible river me…
monuments.nepaliSummary: ब्रह्मायणी पनौतीकी रक्षक मातृदेवी हुन्; उनको मन्दिर दोभान नजिक छ र पनौती जात्रामा उनको रथ तानिन्छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Tell the legend of the invisible river and the goddess's chariot.

features: three-tiered pagoda in a forested hilltop complex above Sankhu
stone stairway climbing through the forest
monuments.disambiguationTip: Sankhu's Bajrayogini is a three-roofed pagoda in a forest above Sankhu in the north-east of the valley; Pharping's Vajrayogini is in the south-west near Padmasambhava's caves.

lore.title: The Goddess Above Sankhu
lore.excerpt: On a forested hillside above the old Newar town of Sankhu, in the north-eastern corner of the Kathmandu Valley, stands the temple complex of Bajrayogini, one of the four Vajrayogini shrines traditionally honoured in the valley. Sankhu, known in Newar as Sakwa,…

lore.title: A Temple in the Forest
lore.excerpt: The Bajrayogini complex is reached by a stone stairway that climbs through the forest from Sankhu, passing shrines and resting places along the way. At the top, a courtyard holds the main three-tiered pagoda, with gilded roofs, carved struts and gilded toranas…

lore.title: Vajrayogini, Tantric Wisdom
lore.excerpt: Vajrayogini is a Tantric deity in Vajrayana Buddhism, a dakini or female embodiment of enlightened wisdom, often depicted dancing, red in colour, holding a skull cup and a curved knife. She represents the transformation of passion into wisdom and is a central …

lore.title: Pilgrims, Festivals and Tantric Worship
lore.excerpt: Bajrayogini is visited by pilgrims from across the valley, and the climb through the forest is part of the devotional experience. Sankhu's main festival, held in spring, includes a procession in which the goddess is carried down from the hilltop to the town, b…

lore.title: Sankhu After the Earthquake
lore.excerpt: Sankhu was one of the most severely damaged towns in the 2015 earthquake, with much of its old town destroyed and many lives lost. The Bajrayogini complex on the hillside was also damaged, and its restoration has been part of the long recovery of the area. Rec…

monuments.audioHook: Climb the stone stairway through the forest above Sankhu, and the sound of the town falls away until you hear only birds and temple bells. At the top waits Bajrayogini, a Tantric goddess of wisdom honoured by Buddhists and Hindus alike, in a three-roofed temple glinting with gold among the trees. Sankhu once stood on t…
monuments.nepaliSummary: साँखुको वज्रयोगिनी मन्दिर जङ्गलले घेरिएको डाँडामा रहेको, बौद्ध र हिन्दु दुवैले पुज्ने तान्त्रिक देवीको तीन तले मन्दिर हो।
monuments.talkingPoint: End with the four Vajrayoginis and Sankhu's role on the Tibet trade route.

features: sunken open-air shrine in a forested ravine at a stream confluence
long queues of devotees on the stairway down to the shrine
monuments.disambiguationTip: Dakshinkali is an open-air shrine at the bottom of a forested ravine south of Pharping; Guhyeshwari is a walled courtyard temple on the Bagmati at Pashupati.

lore.title: Kali of the South
lore.excerpt: Dakshinkali, 'Kali of the south', is one of the most important goddess shrines in Nepal, set in a forested ravine at the meeting of two streams below the town of Pharping, on the southern edge of the Kathmandu Valley. Tradition associates its establishment wit…

lore.title: A Shrine at the Bottom of a Ravine
lore.excerpt: Dakshinkali's setting is its most striking architectural feature. A long stairway descends from the road into a wooded ravine, where the shrine stands at the confluence of two streams, open to the sky rather than enclosed in a tiered temple. The sanctum is cov…

lore.title: The Fierce Mother
lore.excerpt: Kali is the fierce, dark form of the great goddess, often depicted with a garland of skulls, a protruding tongue and weapons in her many hands, standing over the body of Shiva. At Dakshinkali the goddess is represented by a black stone image within the sanctum…

lore.title: Tuesdays, Saturdays and Dashain
lore.excerpt: Dakshinkali is busiest on Tuesdays and Saturdays, the days traditionally favoured for worshipping the goddess here, when thousands of devotees come to make offerings and, in many cases, to sacrifice animals, usually male goats and chickens, through the shrine'…

lore.title: Managing Crowds in a Ravine
lore.excerpt: Dakshinkali's popularity creates significant management challenges. The ravine setting concentrates crowds on narrow stairways, and safety measures such as railings and queue management are essential on busy days. Waste from offerings and picnics, along with t…

monuments.audioHook: Follow the long stairway down into this forested ravine, and the air grows cooler as two streams meet below you. Here, at the bottom, is Dakshinkali, Kali of the south, one of the most powerful goddess shrines in Nepal. Tradition says King Pratap Malla built it after the goddess appeared to him in a dream. Kali is the …
monuments.nepaliSummary: दक्षिणकाली फर्पिङ नजिकैको खोल्सामा रहेको कालीको प्रसिद्ध शक्तिपीठ हो, जहाँ मंगलबार र शनिबार ठूलो भीड लाग्छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Begin in Kali's ravine and explain sacrifice and the family feast.

monuments.disambiguationTip: Jal Binayak is a three-roofed riverside pagoda at the Chobhar gorge; Karya Binayak is a small hilltop shrine and Ashok Binayak a tiny gilded shrine in Kathmandu.

lore.title: Ganesh at the Valley's Outlet
lore.excerpt: Jal Binayak, 'Ganesh of the water', stands on the bank of the Bagmati river at Chobhar, where the river leaves the Kathmandu Valley through a narrow gorge. The temple is traditionally dated to 1602, though this should be confirmed from inscriptions, and it is …

lore.title: A Pagoda Above the Gorge
lore.excerpt: Jal Binayak is a three-tiered pagoda with carved struts, wooden doors and gilded elements, raised on a plinth near the river. Its roof struts are carved with deities, and the temple is surrounded by a small courtyard and shrines. The setting is dramatic: the B…

lore.title: The Rock That Is Ganesh
lore.excerpt: As at several of the valley's important Ganesh shrines, the god at Jal Binayak is worshipped in the form of a natural rock rather than a carved statue, understood as a self-manifested form of the elephant-headed remover of obstacles. The rock is covered in red…

lore.title: Tuesday Prayers by the River
lore.excerpt: Jal Binayak receives regular worship, especially on Tuesdays, sacred to Ganesh in Nepal, when devotees from nearby towns and from Kathmandu come to pray. Ganesh Chaturthi, the god's festival, brings larger crowds. Devotees offer red powder, flowers, sweets and…

lore.title: A Sacred River in Trouble
lore.excerpt: Jal Binayak's setting beside the Bagmati exposes it to the river's problems: pollution from the city upstream, floods during the monsoon and changes to the riverbank caused by development and quarrying. The water flowing through the gorge carries much of the v…

monuments.audioHook: Stand by this three-roofed temple and listen to the Bagmati rushing through the narrow gorge below. Legend says this is exactly where Manjushri raised his sword and cut the hills, letting the ancient lake drain away so that the Kathmandu Valley could be born. Geologists agree the valley really was once a lake. Guarding…
monuments.nepaliSummary: चोभारको जल विनायक बागमती खोँचको छेउमा रहेको तीन तले गणेश मन्दिर हो, जहाँ मञ्जुश्रीले उपत्यकाको ताल निकासेको किंवदन्ती छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Stand at the gorge of the lake legend before heading on to Khokana.

riverside shrines, rest houses and cremation platforms
monuments.disambiguationTip: Tribeni Ghat is a riverside confluence with stone steps and small shrines; Brahmayani is the goddess temple beside it, and Arya Ghat is at Pashupati on the Bagmati.

lore.title: Where Three Rivers Meet
lore.excerpt: Tribeni Ghat in Panauti marks the confluence of the Roshi and Punyamati rivers, joined, according to tradition, by a third, invisible river called the Lilavati, so that the place is a tribeni, a meeting of three rivers. Confluences are especially sacred in Hin…

lore.title: Steps, Shrines and Rest Houses
lore.excerpt: The ghat consists of stone steps descending to the water at the confluence, with small shrines, lingams and images set along the banks. Rest houses, known as patis and sattals, provide shelter for pilgrims and for families attending cremations, which take plac…

lore.title: The Invisible River
lore.excerpt: The idea of an invisible third river echoes the famous confluence at Prayag in India, where the Ganga and Yamuna are said to meet the hidden Saraswati. At Panauti, the invisible Lilavati completes the sacred triad, and local legends tell stories of its origin,…

lore.title: Makar Mela and Everyday Rites
lore.excerpt: Every twelve years, Tribeni Ghat hosts the Makar Mela, a great bathing festival in the month of Magh, when the sun enters Capricorn and pilgrims from across Nepal and beyond come to bathe in the confluence over several weeks. The festival transforms the quiet …

lore.title: Floods and Fragile Banks
lore.excerpt: The ghat's riverside location exposes it to monsoon floods, which can erode the banks, damage steps and undermine shrines. Changes in river flow caused by upstream development, sand mining and changes in land use add to these pressures, and pollution threatens…

monuments.audioHook: Walk down the stone steps to the water, where two rivers meet below the old town of Panauti. Locals will tell you there is a third river here too, the Lilavati, which no one can see. monuments.nepaliSummary: पनौतीको त्रिवेणी घाट रोशी र पुण्यमाती नदी र अदृश्य लीलावतीको दोभान हो, जहाँ बाह्र वर्षमा मकर मेला लाग्छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Walk the ghat between Panauti's two great temples and explain the three-river confluence.

monuments.disambiguationTip: Look for the red-cloaked Hanuman under an umbrella at the gate; Gaddhi Baithak is the white European-style facade, and Taleju is the tall triple-roofed temple on a stepped plinth.

lore.title: Seat of Malla and Shah Kings
lore.excerpt: Hanuman Dhoka was the royal palace of Kathmandu from the Malla period until the Shah court moved to Narayanhiti in the late nineteenth century. Parts of the complex are older, but its present character owes most to King Pratap Malla, who ruled Kantipur in the …

lore.title: Courtyards, Towers and Carved Windows
lore.excerpt: The palace is not one building but a sequence of brick courtyards, or chowks, linked by low doorways and wrapped in carved timber. Visitors enter through the painted gate beside the Hanuman statue into Nasal Chowk, a long rectangular court whose name is linked…

lore.title: Hanuman, Narasimha and the Gate
lore.excerpt: The monkey god Hanuman stands guard beside the main gate, his image so thickly coated in red sindoor paste and mustard oil that his features have disappeared beneath generations of offerings. He wears a red cloak and shelters under a royal umbrella, signalling…

lore.title: Dashain Sacrifices and the Kumari's Blessing
lore.excerpt: Although no king has lived here for more than a century, the palace still sits at the centre of Kathmandu's ritual calendar. During Dashain, sacrifices are offered in the inner palace courtyards to Taleju, the royal goddess whose temple rises from the palace g…

lore.title: Earthquake Damage and Reconstruction
lore.excerpt: The 2015 Gorkha earthquake struck Hanuman Dhoka hard. The upper storeys of the nine-storey Basantapur tower were badly damaged, several palace wings cracked, and temples in the surrounding square collapsed. Reconstruction has been led by the Department of Arch…

monuments.audioHook: Look to the left of the gate and you will see a figure with no face at all, only a red, rounded shape wrapped in a cloak beneath an umbrella. monuments.talkingPoint: Explain how the Hanuman statue named the palace and why four towers honour four cities.

tall stepped brick plinth

monuments.disambiguationTip: Taleju is the tallest roofline and sits inside a walled enclosure; Maju Dega also has a stepped plinth but stands open on the square with tiled roofs and a Nandi bull in front.

lore.title: The Goddess Who Came with the Kings
lore.excerpt: Taleju Bhawani was the tutelary goddess of the Malla kings, and her cult reached the Kathmandu Valley with the dynasty's ancestors from the south, by tradition through King Harisimhadeva of Tirhut in the fourteenth century. In 1564 King Mahendra Malla built th…

lore.title: Tallest Roofline in the Square
lore.excerpt: Taleju rises in three gilded copper roofs above a stepped brick plinth, making it the highest building in Kathmandu Durbar Square and the landmark that orients visitors from every side. The plinth raises the shrine far above street level, which both protects i…

lore.title: A Goddess Kept from View
lore.excerpt: Taleju is understood as a form of Durga, the warrior goddess who destroys demons, and she is closely linked with the Tantric goddesses of the Newar tradition. Her image is never displayed to the public, and the sanctum is served by a small number of designated…

lore.title: Opened Once a Year
lore.excerpt: For most of the year the Taleju temple is closed, but on Maha Navami, the ninth day of Dashain, it opens to Hindu worshippers, who queue for hours across the square for a rare chance to enter. Animal sacrifices are offered to the goddess during Dashain in the …

lore.title: Surviving the 2015 Earthquake
lore.excerpt: Taleju came through the 2015 Gorkha earthquake better than many of its neighbours, which some residents interpret as a sign of the goddess's protection and engineers attribute to its massive plinth and careful original construction. The temple still required i…

monuments.audioHook: Turn your eyes upward until you find the highest golden roof in the square. That is Taleju, the royal goddess of the Malla kings, and in 1564 King Mahendra Malla built her temple so tall that, legend says, no one in Kathmandu was allowed to build higher. Here is the remarkable part: almost no one has ever seen her. The…

monuments.disambiguationTip: Kasthamandap is open at ground level with no enclosed sanctum walls and its timber looks newer than its neighbours; Trailokya Mohan and Maju Dega are closed temples on taller plinths.

lore.title: The Pavilion That Named a City
lore.excerpt: Kasthamandap, meaning 'wooden pavilion', is the building from which Kathmandu takes its name. Chronicles tell that it was raised from the timber of a single sal tree, a story that captures how prodigious its beams seemed to later generations. For centuries sch…

lore.title: A Building Without Walls
lore.excerpt: Unlike the closed temples around it, Kasthamandap is essentially a timber frame on a brick platform: three storeys of posts, beams and roofs, open on the ground floor so that people can gather, sit and pass through. Its structure depends on interlocking joiner…

lore.title: Gorakhnath at the Centre
lore.excerpt: At the heart of the ground floor sits an image of Gorakhnath, the great yogi of the Nath tradition, who is revered by both Hindus and Buddhists in Kathmandu. Nath legends describe Gorakhnath as a disciple of Matsyendranath, the rain-bringing deity whom Newar B…

lore.title: Singing, Feasting and Festival Gatherings
lore.excerpt: As a public pavilion, Kasthamandap has always been a place where neighbourhood groups meet. Devotional singing groups gather here in the evenings, and feasts and religious readings are held during festivals. Its position on the processional route at Maru means…

lore.title: A Community-Led Rebuilding
lore.excerpt: Kasthamandap collapsed completely on 25 April 2015, killing people who had sheltered beneath it, and its loss became a symbol of the earthquake's damage to Kathmandu's heritage. Before rebuilding, archaeologists from Durham University and UNESCO worked with th…

monuments.audioHook: Stand at Maru and look at the open wooden pavilion in front of you. This is Kasthamandap, the wooden shelter that gave Kathmandu its name. monuments.disambiguationTip: Kumari Ghar is a red-brick house with carved windows and lion guardians at the doorway; Shiva Parvati Mandir has two painted figures leaning from an upper window, and Gaddhi Baithak is white neoclassical.

lore.title: A Palace for a Living Goddess
lore.excerpt: Kumari Ghar was built in 1757 by Jaya Prakash Malla, the last Malla king of Kathmandu, as the residence of the Royal Kumari, a young girl worshipped as the living embodiment of the goddess Taleju. The king's devotion to the Kumari was famous, and he is credite…

lore.title: Newar Courtyard Craft
lore.excerpt: The building follows the plan of a Newar Buddhist monastery: a three-storey brick block wrapped around a square inner courtyard. Its facades are among the finest examples of eighteenth-century Newar woodcarving, with lattice windows, carved frames and projecti…

lore.title: Taleju in a Child's Form
lore.excerpt: The Kumari is understood as Taleju, the royal goddess, dwelling in the body of a girl from the Shakya clan of Kathmandu's Newar Buddhist community. She is chosen in early childhood after examinations of her horoscope, health and physical signs, described in tr…

lore.title: Glimpses at the Window and Indra Jatra
lore.excerpt: Visitors who wait quietly in the courtyard may see the Kumari appear for a moment at the carved window on the upper floor, but photographing her is strictly forbidden and her caretakers enforce the rule. Her greatest public appearance comes during Indra Jatra,…

lore.title: Surviving the Earthquake, Changing Traditions
lore.excerpt: Kumari Ghar came through the 2015 earthquake with relatively limited damage while temples a few steps away collapsed, and many residents took this as evidence of the goddess's protection. The building still needed careful inspection, repair of cracked masonry …

monuments.audioHook: Step through the lion-guarded doorway into this small courtyard and look up at the carved window on the top floor. If you are patient and quiet, a young girl dressed in red, with a painted third eye, may appear for a few seconds. monuments.talkingPoint: Explain how the Kumari is chosen and how the 1768 Indra Jatra conquest unfolded.

black, red and yellow paint refreshed by devotees
low railed enclosure open to the sky
monuments.disambiguationTip: Kal Bhairav is a full-body stone image standing in the open; Swet Bhairav is a gilded mask behind a wooden lattice screen a few steps east.

lore.title: The Image Found in a Field
lore.excerpt: Kal Bhairav is one of the largest stone sculptures in Kathmandu, a towering image of Bhairav, the fierce manifestation of Shiva. Tradition says it was found in a field north of the city and brought to the palace square in the seventeenth century by King Pratap…

lore.title: Carving a Colossus
lore.excerpt: Unlike most images in the square, Kal Bhairav is not housed in a temple. He stands in the open within a low enclosure, carved in high relief from stone and painted in vivid black, red and yellow that devotees refresh regularly. The figure is roughly three metr…

lore.title: Weapons, Skulls and the Defeat of Ignorance
lore.excerpt: Bhairav embodies Shiva's power to destroy, but in Newar belief that destruction protects devotees and cuts away ignorance and ego. This image shows him with multiple arms bearing weapons and ritual objects, including a sword and a skull cup, and wearing a garl…

lore.title: Do Not Lie Before Bhairav
lore.excerpt: Kal Bhairav is famous as Kathmandu's god of truth. Tradition holds that anyone who lies in front of the image will vomit blood and die, and for centuries people were brought here to swear oaths during disputes, sometimes before officials of the royal court in …

lore.title: Protecting a Painted Stone

lore.excerpt: The great gilded mask of Swet Bhairav, the White Bhairav, was installed in 1795 by King Rana Bahadur Shah, a grandson of Prithvi Narayan Shah. Rana Bahadur's reign was turbulent, marked by palace intrigue and later by his abdication and exile, but his patronag…

lore.title: The Mask Behind the Screen
lore.excerpt: Swet Bhairav is not a free-standing temple but a shrine built into the wall of a building, where the enormous mask is kept behind a carved wooden lattice screen. For most of the year visitors can only glimpse its golden surface through the openings. The mask i…

lore.title: The White Bhairav's Face
lore.excerpt: Bhairav is the fierce form of Shiva, and in the Newar tradition he appears in many guises, each with its own character and shrine. Swet Bhairav, the 'White Bhairav', is depicted here as a vast face with staring eyes, sharp fangs and a crown decorated with skul…

lore.title: Rice Beer from a God's Mouth
lore.excerpt: Swet Bhairav comes alive during Indra Jatra, the eight-day festival in late summer that honours Indra, the god of rain, and marks the end of the monsoon. On the festival days the wooden screen is opened, the mask is decorated, and jaand, the local rice beer, f…

lore.excerpt: Gilded copper is more durable than wood, but it still requires careful attention. Pollution, humidity and handling can tarnish the gilding, and the metal can be dented during festival crowds. The wooden screen that protects the mask also needs maintenance, as …

monuments.audioHook: Look closely at the wooden lattice screen in the wall in front of you. Behind it hides a giant golden face with fangs and staring eyes: Swet Bhairav, the White Bhairav, installed by King Rana Bahadur Shah in 1795. For most of the year he stays hidden, but during the Indra Jatra festival the screen swings open and rice …
monuments.nepaliSummary: श्वेत भैरवको सुनौलो विशाल मुकुण्डो राजा रणबहादुर शाहले सन् १७९५ मा राखेका हुन्; इन्द्रजात्रामा यसको मुखबाट जाँड बग्छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Contrast the hidden mask with Kal Bhairav and describe the rice beer ritual.

features: two-tiered pagoda on a three-stage plinth
explicit erotic carvings on the lower struts
stands directly beside the Hanuman Dhoka gate
monuments.disambiguationTip: Jagannath is the two-roofed temple beside the palace gate with erotic carvings on its struts; Maju Dega and Trailokya Mohan have three roofs and stand further south-west.

lore.title: Among the Oldest in the Square
lore.excerpt: The Jagannath temple is often described as one of the oldest structures in this part of Kathmandu Durbar Square, though its precise date is debated. Many accounts attribute it to the reign of King Mahendra Malla in the sixteenth century, while others associate…

lore.title: Two Roofs and a Stepped Plinth
lore.excerpt: Jagannath is a classic Newar pagoda: a square brick sanctum raised on a stepped plinth, with two tiers of sloping roofs supported by carved wooden struts. The plinth lifts the temple above the bustle of the street and provides a platform on which worshippers c…

lore.title: Why the Erotic Carvings?
lore.excerpt: The erotic carvings on Jagannath's struts surprise many visitors, and guides are often asked to explain them. There is no single answer. One popular story claims that the images protect the temple from lightning, because the goddess of lightning is a shy virgi…

lore.title: Daily Worship by the Palace Gate
lore.excerpt: Jagannath receives daily worship from priests and local devotees, who make offerings of flowers, rice, incense and coloured powder. Because of its location beside the Hanuman Dhoka gate, it lies on the route of many festivals in the square. During Indra Jatra,…

lore.title: Holding Up the Struts
lore.excerpt: Like many temples in the square, Jagannath was damaged in the 2015 earthquake and required repair. Wooden struts are the most fragile part of a Newar pagoda: they carry the weight of the roof eaves while being exposed to rain, sun and insects, and some of the …

monuments.audioHook: Look up under the roof of this two-tiered temple beside the palace gate, and you may need a moment to understand what the carvings show. On the struts of Jagannath, the Lord of the World, gods stand above scenes of couples in explicit embrace. One local story says these carvings protect the temple from lightning, becau…
monuments.nepaliSummary: जगन्नाथ मन्दिर हनुमानढोका नजिकैको दुई तले प्यागोडा हो, जसका टुँडालमा कोरिएका कामुक मूर्ति प्रसिद्ध छन्।
monuments.talkingPoint: Discuss the competing explanations of the erotic carvings.

features: large bronze bell suspended in a sturdy frame on a raised platform
pair of great ceremonial drums installed nearby in 1800
monuments.disambiguationTip: This bell stands on a raised platform in Kathmandu's square opposite the Jagannath temple; Patan's Taleju Bell hangs between two thick pillars in front of the Patan palace.

lore.title: A Bell for the Royal Goddess
lore.excerpt: The great bell in Kathmandu Durbar Square was hung in 1797 by King Rana Bahadur Shah, in the early decades of Shah rule over the valley. It was dedicated to Taleju, the royal tutelary goddess whose temple rises nearby, and its installation continued a Malla tr…

lore.title: Casting and Hanging a Giant
lore.excerpt: The bell is cast in bronze and hangs in a sturdy frame on a raised platform, high enough for its sound to carry across the square and beyond. Casting a bell of this size was a major undertaking, requiring skilled metalworkers, large quantities of metal and a c…

lore.title: Sound as Offering
lore.excerpt: In Hindu and Buddhist worship, sound is itself an offering and a means of purification. The ringing of bells drives away negative forces, announces the presence of the deity and calls devotees to attention. A great bell dedicated to Taleju therefore extends th…

lore.title: Ringing for Taleju
lore.excerpt: The bell is traditionally rung during the worship of Taleju, its deep tone joining the drums, conch shells and chanting that accompany the goddess's rituals. On festival days, when processions and dances fill the square, the sound of the bell adds to an atmosp…

lore.title: Keeping the Frame Sound
lore.excerpt: Bronze bells are durable, but the frames and platforms that carry them need maintenance. Timber beams can weaken through rot or insect damage, and the weight of the bell places constant stress on the joints. The 2015 earthquake shook the platform along with ev…

monuments.audioHook: Look for the great bronze bell hanging high on its platform. King Rana Bahadur Shah hung it here in 1797 for Taleju, the royal goddess, and a few years later his son added the two huge drums nearby. Together they were the voice of the palace: rung and beaten during the goddess's worship, their sound was believed to dri…
monuments.nepaliSummary: तलेजु घण्ट राजा रणबहादुर शाहले सन् १७९७ मा तलेजु देवीका लागि झुण्ड्याएका हुन्; नजिकै गीर्वाणयुद्ध विक्रम शाहका ठूला नगरा छन्।
monuments.talkingPoint: Link the bell and drums to early Shah patronage of Taleju.

features: long dark stone slab set into the outer palace wall
many scripts side by side, including Devanagari, Persian and Roman letters
European words such as WINTER carved among South Asian scripts
monuments.disambiguationTip: This is a flat stone slab set into a palace wall near the Hanuman gate; the Manadeva inscription at Changu Narayan is carved on a free-standing pillar.

lore.title: A Poet-King's Signature
lore.excerpt: King Pratap Malla, who ruled Kathmandu from 1641 to 1674, took pride in being a scholar and poet and styled himself Kavindra, 'king of poets'. In 1664 he set this stone inscription into the wall of his palace. It contains a hymn to the goddess Kalika and is fa…

lore.title: A Wall of Words
lore.excerpt: The inscription is carved on a long slab of dark stone set into the outer wall of Hanuman Dhoka palace, at a height where passers-by can read it but not easily touch it. Its surface is divided into lines of text in different scripts, with careful spacing that …

lore.title: A Hymn to Kalika
lore.excerpt: Though often admired as a linguistic curiosity, the inscription is above all a devotional poem addressed to Kalika, a form of the goddess Kali who protects against danger and embodies the power of time and transformation. Pratap Malla was a devotee of several …

lore.title: The Spout That Would Flow with Milk
lore.excerpt: A popular legend surrounds the inscription. It is said that if anyone succeeds in reading the entire text, in all its languages, milk will flow from the spout in the wall instead of water. No one, the story goes, has ever managed it, and the legend has become …

lore.title: Weathering and Legibility
lore.excerpt: Stone inscriptions face a slow but serious threat: weathering that erodes the sharp edges of letters until texts become illegible. Rain, pollution, temperature changes and touching all contribute. Pratap Malla's inscription has fared reasonably well, but parts…

monuments.audioHook: Find the long dark stone set into the palace wall, near the Hanuman gate. In 1664 King Pratap Malla, who called himself the king of poets, carved a hymn to the goddess Kalika here in many scripts and languages, traditionally counted as fifteen. Look carefully and you may spot something unexpected: European letters spel…
monuments.nepaliSummary: राजा प्रताप मल्लले सन् १६६४ मा १५ भाषाका लिपिमा कालिकाको स्तुति कुँदेको यो शिलालेख हनुमानढोकाको पर्खालमा छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Challenge guests to find the European words, then tell the milk legend.

features: three-tiered pagoda on a stepped plinth
large kneeling Garuda statue in front
fresh post-2015 timber alongside salvaged old carvings
monuments.disambiguationTip: Look for the kneeling Garuda facing the temple: Trailokya Mohan belongs to Vishnu, while nearby Maju Dega is Shiva's and has a Nandi bull instead.

lore.title: A Brother's Memorial
lore.excerpt: Trailokya Mohan Narayan, meaning 'Narayan, enchanter of the three worlds', was built in 1680 by King Parthivendra Malla in memory of his elder brother, King Nripendra Malla, who had died young. The temple stands near Kasthamandap on the south-western side of K…

lore.title: Three Roofs Over a Stepped Plinth
lore.excerpt: Trailokya Mohan follows the classic three-tiered Newar pagoda form, with a square sanctum on a stepped plinth and three sloping roofs that diminish in size as they rise. The plinth raises the temple above street level and gives it presence on the square, while…

lore.title: The Ten Avatars of Vishnu
lore.excerpt: The roof struts of Trailokya Mohan depict the ten avatars of Vishnu, the forms he takes to restore order to the world: Matsya the fish, Kurma the tortoise, Varaha the boar, Narasimha the man-lion, Vamana the dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha and Kalki.…

lore.title: Dances of the Ten Avatars
lore.excerpt: During Indra Jatra, the great late-summer festival of Kathmandu, a performance of the ten avatars of Vishnu is staged on the platform in front of Trailokya Mohan. Masked dancers enact the avatars, bringing the carvings on the temple's struts to life for crowds…

lore.title: Collapse and Rebuilding
lore.excerpt: Trailokya Mohan was among the temples that collapsed completely in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, leaving only its plinth and a pile of brick and timber. Salvage teams recovered carved struts, doors and other elements from the debris, numbering and storing them f…

monuments.audioHook: In front of this temple, a stone Garuda kneels with his hands pressed together, gazing at the sanctum. He is the bird-mount of Vishnu, and he tells you exactly whose temple this is. Trailokya Mohan, the enchanter of the three worlds, was built in 1680 by King Parthivendra Malla to honour his brother, a king who died yo…
monuments.nepaliSummary: त्रैलोक्य मोहन नारायण मन्दिर राजा पार्थिवेन्द्र मल्लले सन् १६८० मा बनाएका हुन्; २०१५ को भूकम्पमा ढलेपछि पुनर्निर्माण गरिएको हो।
monuments.talkingPoint: Match the strut carvings to the ten avatars and point out salvaged pieces.

features: three-tiered pagoda on a tall nine-stage plinth
plinth steps crowded with seated people
gilded pinnacle above tiled roofs
monuments.disambiguationTip: Maju Dega has the tallest stepped plinth in the open square, usually covered with seated people, and a Nandi bull rather than a Garuda in front.

lore.title: A Queen Mother's Temple
lore.excerpt: Maju Dega, often translated as 'the temple of the mother', was built in 1690 by Queen Riddhi Lakshmi, the mother of King Bhupalendra Malla. Riddhi Lakshmi was one of the most influential royal women of Malla Kathmandu, acting as regent and patron during her so…

lore.title: Nine Steps to the Sky
lore.excerpt: Maju Dega's most striking feature is its tall plinth of nine stepped stages, which lifts the three-tiered temple high above the square. From the top of the steps, visitors gain one of the best views over Kathmandu Durbar Square, which is why the plinth is almo…

lore.title: Shiva's Lingam and Nandi
lore.excerpt: Inside the sanctum is a Shiva lingam, the abstract column that represents Shiva's creative energy and presence, set in a yoni base symbolising Shakti, the feminine power. Facing the temple stands Nandi, the bull who serves as Shiva's vehicle and devoted attend…

lore.title: The City's Grandstand
lore.excerpt: Maju Dega is both a shrine and a gathering place. In the mornings, devotees climb the steps to offer flowers, rice and water to the lingam, and the sound of bells mingles with conversation. Through the day, the plinth becomes Kathmandu's grandstand: people sit…

lore.title: Standing Through 2015
lore.excerpt: Maju Dega survived the 2015 earthquake while neighbouring Trailokya Mohan and Kasthamandap collapsed. Its survival has been attributed to the robustness of its tall brick plinth and the quality of its original construction, although it still required inspectio…

monuments.audioHook: If you want the best view in Kathmandu Durbar Square, climb the nine steps of this temple and sit with the locals. You are on Maju Dega, built in 1690 by Queen Riddhi Lakshmi, a royal mother who helped rule Kathmandu while her son was a child. Inside is a Shiva lingam, and the bull Nandi waits faithfully in front. Look…
monuments.nepaliSummary: माजु देग रानी ऋद्धिलक्ष्मीले सन् १६९० मा बनाएको शिव मन्दिर हो, जसको नौ तले चबुतराबाट दरबार क्षेत्रको राम्रो दृश्य देखिन्छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Invite guests to sit on the plinth while telling the queen mother's story.

features: rectangular two-storey house-like temple on a stepped plinth
central upper window with a divine couple looking down on the square
monuments.disambiguationTip: Look for the painted couple at the central upper window; Kumari Ghar has carved windows but no figures, and Gaddhi Baithak is white stucco.

lore.title: A Shah Regent's Gift
lore.excerpt: The Shiva Parvati temple was built in the late eighteenth century by Bahadur Shah, a son of Prithvi Narayan Shah who served as regent for his young nephew, King Rana Bahadur Shah. It belongs to the first generation of Shah patronage in Kathmandu after the conq…

lore.title: A Temple in the Form of a House
lore.excerpt: The temple is built as a rectangular two-storey structure on a stepped plinth, resembling the residential buildings of Newar towns more than the tall pagodas nearby. Its ground floor has carved doors and windows, while the upper storey features a central windo…

lore.title: The Divine Couple at the Window
lore.excerpt: The temple's famous image shows Shiva and Parvati, the divine couple of Hindu mythology, leaning from the upper window as if watching the bustle of the square below. The figures are carved in wood and brightly painted, Shiva recognisable by his trident and mat…

lore.title: Gods Who Watch the Festivals
lore.excerpt: The Shiva Parvati temple is less a focus of intense ritual than a beloved presence in the square. Devotees offer flowers and prayers at its doors, and couples sometimes visit to ask the divine pair for a happy marriage. During festivals such as Teej, when wome…

lore.title: Caring for Painted Wood
lore.excerpt: The painted wooden figures of Shiva and Parvati are vulnerable to sun, rain and pollution, and their colours must be periodically renewed by skilled painters using traditional or compatible pigments. Conservators try to strike a balance between keeping the fig…

monuments.audioHook: Look up at the centre window of the small temple in front of you, and you will see two figures leaning out, watching the crowd just as you are watching them. They are Shiva and Parvati, the divine couple, carved in wood and brightly painted. This temple was built in the late eighteenth century by Bahadur Shah, son of t…
monuments.nepaliSummary: शिव पार्वती मन्दिरको माथिल्लो झ्यालबाट शिव र पार्वतीका रङ्गीन काठे मूर्ति दरबार क्षेत्रतिर हेरिरहेका देखिन्छन्।
monuments.talkingPoint: Point out the divine couple and discuss early Shah patronage.

features: white neoclassical facade with columns and pediments
European-style wing attached to the traditional Newar palace
first-floor balcony overlooking Basantapur
monuments.disambiguationTip: Gaddhi Baithak is the only white European-style facade in the square; Hanuman Dhoka's gate is brick and gilt with the red Hanuman beside it.

lore.title: A Rana Statement in Stucco
lore.excerpt: Gaddhi Baithak was built in 1908 by Chandra Shumsher Rana, the hereditary prime minister who governed Nepal during the Rana era, when the Shah kings were figureheads and real power lay with the Rana family. Its name means 'throne seat', and it served as a hall…

lore.title: Columns Among the Pagodas
lore.excerpt: Gaddhi Baithak's white facade, with classical columns, pediments and symmetrical windows, contrasts dramatically with the brick and timber pagodas around it. It was built with brick walls coated in lime plaster and stucco, techniques that the Ranas used widely…

lore.title: Symbols of a Modernising Regime
lore.excerpt: Gaddhi Baithak carries no deity images in the manner of the temples around it. Its iconography is political rather than religious. The European columns and symmetrical facade stood for order, modernity and connection with the wider world, ideas that the Rana p…

lore.title: Watching Indra Jatra from the Balcony
lore.excerpt: Gaddhi Baithak's most important ritual role comes during Indra Jatra, when the head of state traditionally watches the festivities from the palace and receives the tika blessing of the Kumari. During the monarchy this was the king's role, and since 2008 the Pr…

lore.title: Retrofitting a Rana Palace
lore.excerpt: Gaddhi Baithak was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquake, which cracked its walls and threatened the stability of its facade. Its construction, brick walls finished with heavy plaster ornament, was vulnerable to shaking, and parts of the stucco decoration fell.…

monuments.audioHook: Among the brick temples and golden roofs, one building looks as if it belongs in London: the white, columned facade of Gaddhi Baithak. It was built in 1908 by Chandra Shumsher Rana, the powerful prime minister who ruled Nepal while the kings were figureheads, in the same year he travelled to Britain. Its name means thr…
monuments.nepaliSummary: गद्दी बैठक सन् १९०८ मा चन्द्रशमशेर राणाले युरोपेली शैलीमा बनाएको दरबार भवन हो, जहाँबाट राष्ट्रप्रमुखले इन्द्रजात्रा हेर्छन्।
monuments.talkingPoint: Use the facade to explain the Rana century and Indra Jatra protocol.

features: compact square shrine topped by a bell-shaped gumbhaj dome
three-stage plinth in the quieter northern square
monuments.disambiguationTip: Kotilingeshwara is a single small domed shrine in Kathmandu's northern square; the Pandra Shivalaya at Pashupatinath are a row of fifteen similar domed shrines on a riverbank.

lore.title: An Early Shrine in the Northern Square
lore.excerpt: Kotilingeshwara Mahadev stands in the quieter northern part of Kathmandu Durbar Square, away from the crowds of Basantapur. It is usually attributed to the reign of King Mahendra Malla in the sixteenth century, making it one of the earlier surviving shrines in…

lore.title: A Dome Among Pagodas
lore.excerpt: Unlike most temples in the square, Kotilingeshwara is not a tiered pagoda but a compact square shrine topped by a bell-shaped dome, a form known in Nepal as gumbhaj. This style, which shows influence from the architecture of northern India, appears in a number…

lore.title: Ten Million Lingams in One
lore.excerpt: The sanctum contains a Shiva lingam, the abstract form of the god that represents his boundless creative energy. The temple's name, 'Lord of ten million lingams', expresses the idea that this single lingam contains the presence of countless others, a way of de…

lore.title: Quiet Daily Worship
lore.excerpt: Kotilingeshwara receives daily offerings from local devotees, especially on Mondays, the day sacred to Shiva, and during festivals such as Maha Shivaratri, when Shiva temples across the valley are crowded with worshippers. Offerings include water, milk, flower…

lore.title: Protecting a Small Monument
lore.excerpt: Small shrines like Kotilingeshwara can be overlooked in conservation planning, which tends to focus on the most famous monuments. Yet they are equally part of the World Heritage property and face the same threats: earthquakes, weathering, pollution and the wea…

monuments.audioHook: Step away from the busy southern square to this small domed temple in the north, where the noise softens. Kotilingeshwara Mahadev means Lord of ten million lingams, and inside is a single stone lingam, said to hold the presence of countless others. Built, according to tradition, in the time of King Mahendra Malla in th…
monuments.nepaliSummary: कोटिलिङ्गेश्वर महादेव दरबार क्षेत्रको उत्तरी भागमा रहेको गुम्बज शैलीको शिव मन्दिर हो, जसलाई महेन्द्र मल्लको पालाको मानिन्छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Contrast the domed gumbhaj style with the pagodas before ending at Taleju.

monuments.century: date unconfirmed; worship of the mask long established across the Malla and Shah centuries
features: shrine on the upper floor of a building overlooking Indra Chowk
busy market crossroads with shops at street level
monuments.disambiguationTip: Akash Bhairav is the blue mask in an upper-floor shrine at Indra Chowk; Swet Bhairav is the golden mask behind a lattice screen in Durbar Square.

lore.title: The Sky Bhairav of Indra Chowk
lore.excerpt: A short walk north-east of Kathmandu Durbar Square lies Indra Chowk, one of the old city's busiest crossroads, where an upper-floor shrine houses the mask of Akash Bhairav, the 'sky Bhairav'. Popular tradition identifies the mask with Yalambar, remembered as t…

lore.title: A Shrine Above the Market
lore.excerpt: Unlike the free-standing temples of Durbar Square, Akash Bhairav's shrine occupies the upper floor of a building, above shops that open onto the crossroads. Its facade carries carved and decorated windows and a balcony from which the shrine overlooks the squar…

lore.title: A Blue Face of Bhairav
lore.excerpt: Akash Bhairav is depicted as a large blue face with bulging eyes, fangs and a crown, one of the many forms of Bhairav, the fierce manifestation of Shiva who guards the city. Blue is associated with the sky, hence the name 'sky Bhairav', and with the vastness a…

lore.title: Indra Jatra at the Crossroads
lore.excerpt: During Indra Jatra, the late-summer festival that marks the end of the monsoon, Akash Bhairav's mask is displayed in Indra Chowk, decorated with flowers and surrounded by offerings, and devotees crowd the crossroads to see it. The festival also features the ra…

lore.title: Heritage in a Living Market
lore.excerpt: Akash Bhairav's shrine faces conservation challenges typical of heritage in Kathmandu's commercial core. The building that houses it is shared with shops, and alterations, signage and wiring can affect its historic character. The 2015 earthquake damaged many b…

monuments.audioHook: Look up above the shops at this busy crossroads and you will find a shrine where a huge blue face watches the market below. This is Akash Bhairav, the sky Bhairav, and many in Kathmandu say the face belongs to Yalambar, the first king of the ancient Kirata dynasty. Legend says he went to watch the great war of the Maha…
monuments.nepaliSummary: इन्द्रचोकको आकाश भैरव निलो मुकुण्डो भएको भैरवको स्थान हो, जसलाई किरात राजा यलम्बरको शिर मानिन्छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Leave the square for the market crossroads and the legend of Yalambar's head.

monuments.century: date unconfirmed; among Kathmandu's principal Ganesh shrines for many centuries
features: tiny gilded shrine at the corner of Kasthamandap
constant stream of commuters pausing to pray
monuments.disambiguationTip: Ashok Binayak is the tiny gilded shrine at Kasthamandap's corner; the pavilion itself is a large open timber structure, and Karya Binayak is a hilltop shrine near Bungamati.

lore.title: Kathmandu's Ganesh of Beginnings
lore.excerpt: Ashok Binayak, also called Maru Ganesh after the Maru neighbourhood, is a small but immensely popular Ganesh shrine at the corner of Kasthamandap, at the south-western entrance to Kathmandu Durbar Square. Its name is traditionally linked to an ashoka tree that…

lore.title: A Small Gilded Shrine
lore.excerpt: Ashok Binayak is a compact shrine with a gilded roof and a richly decorated front, set at the corner of the Kasthamandap platform. Its small size means that devotees worship from the street, standing before the image to make offerings, ring the bell and receiv…

lore.title: The Remover of Obstacles
lore.excerpt: Ganesh, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati, is the god of beginnings and the remover of obstacles, worshipped before any important undertaking. His image at Ashok Binayak is covered in red powder and offerings, so that its features are often hidden b…

lore.title: A Prayer on the Way to Work
lore.excerpt: From dawn until late at night, Ashok Binayak receives a constant stream of devotees: commuters on their way to work, families preparing for weddings, students before examinations and travellers before long journeys. Many touch the shrine, ring the bell and rec…

lore.title: Survival Beside a Collapsed Neighbour
lore.excerpt: When Kasthamandap collapsed in the 2015 earthquake, the small Ashok Binayak shrine at its corner survived, and worshippers continued to visit it amid the rubble, a scene that became a symbol of resilience for many residents. The shrine required inspection and …

monuments.audioHook: Before you leave Durbar Square, watch this tiny golden shrine for a minute. Commuters on motorbikes slow down, students touch the step, a family with a new car waits for a blessing. This is Ashok Binayak, also called Maru Ganesh, the elephant-headed remover of obstacles, and Kathmandu residents have stopped here before…
monuments.nepaliSummary: अशोक विनायक (मरु गणेश) काष्ठमण्डपको छेउमा रहेको सानो सुनौलो गणेश मन्दिर हो, जहाँ काठमाडौंवासी यात्रा र नयाँ काम सुरु गर्नुअघि पूजा गर्छन्।
monuments.talkingPoint: Close the loop back at Maru with the Ganesh who blesses every journey.

monuments.century: late 17th century CE (present temple); worship attested in Licchavi inscriptions
features: two-tiered pagoda with gilded copper roofs
large walled courtyard closed to non-Hindus
temple rising above the west bank of the Bagmati
monuments.disambiguationTip: Pashupatinath's gilded two-tier roofs rise above the Bagmati ghats and are seen by non-Hindus from the east-bank terraces; Guhyeshwari is a separate shrine upstream with a serpent-supported golden canopy.

lore.title: Lord of All Creatures
lore.excerpt: Pashupatinath, Shiva as Pashupati, 'lord of all creatures', is the most sacred Hindu shrine in Nepal and one of the most important Shiva temples in the world. Worship of Pashupati is attested in Licchavi inscriptions from the fifth century onward, when the dei…

lore.title: Gold, Silver and a Sacred River
lore.excerpt: The main temple is a two-tiered pagoda with gilded copper roofs, raised on a square plinth and opening on all four sides through silver-plated doors. Its roof struts are carved with deities, and gilded finials crowned with tridents rise from the summit. The te…

lore.title: The Four-Faced Lingam
lore.excerpt: The sanctum houses a lingam with four faces, each representing an aspect of Shiva facing a cardinal direction, while the top of the lingam represents a fifth, formless aspect. The faces are known as Sadyojata, Vamadeva, Tatpurusha and Aghora, with Ishana above…

lore.title: Priests from the South and Maha Shivaratri
lore.excerpt: Pashupatinath's daily rituals are performed by priests known as Bhattas, Brahmins traditionally drawn from Karnataka in southern India, a custom said to date back many centuries and maintained into the present day, alongside local priests and attendants. Worsh…

lore.title: Managing a Living Sacred Landscape
lore.excerpt: The main Pashupatinath temple survived the 2015 earthquake largely intact, a fact many devotees attribute to the god's protection, while some smaller structures in the complex suffered damage and were repaired. The Pashupati Area Development Trust, established…

monuments.audioHook: Look across the Bagmati river at the golden roofs rising above the courtyard walls. That is Pashupatinath, the temple of Shiva as lord of all creatures, the holiest Hindu shrine in Nepal. Kings of the Licchavi age were already honouring this god some fifteen hundred years ago. lore.title: A Small Temple of the Mother Goddess
lore.excerpt: Bachhareshwari, also known as Vatsaleshwari, is a small temple in the Pashupatinath complex, near the ghats on the western bank of the Bagmati. It is dedicated to a form of the goddess understood as a mother protecting her child, and its name is connected with…

lore.title: Carvings at the Edge of the Ghats
lore.excerpt: The temple is a modest structure with brick walls, a carved doorway and roof struts, set among the dense cluster of shrines, rest houses and ghats on the western bank. Its most distinctive features are the carvings on its struts and frames, which depict Tantri…

lore.title: Skeletons and the Mother
lore.excerpt: The skeletal figures carved on Bachhareshwari's struts belong to a Tantric iconography in which death and decay are confronted directly rather than hidden. In Tantric traditions associated with Shiva and the goddess, cremation grounds are powerful places of pr…

lore.title: A Shivaratri Tradition
lore.excerpt: Bachhareshwari is associated in some accounts with rituals performed during Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, when the Pashupati complex fills with pilgrims and sadhus. Guidebooks mention a traditional dance once performed at the temple during the fes…

lore.title: Protecting Small Shrines at Pashupati
lore.excerpt: The Pashupati complex includes hundreds of shrines, many of them small and little documented. Bachhareshwari is one of these, and its carvings are vulnerable to weathering, to smoke from the cremation ghats and to the humidity of the riverbank. The 2015 earthq…

monuments.audioHook: Near the cremation ghats stands a small temple that most visitors walk straight past. Stop and look up at its carvings: skeletons, Tantric figures and lovers, side by side. This is Bachhareshwari, a shrine to a mother goddess whose name recalls a cow caring for her calf. Here, a few steps from the funeral pyres, the ca…
monuments.nepaliSummary: वत्सलेश्वरी (बच्छलेश्वरी) पशुपतिका घाट नजिकैको सानो मन्दिर हो, जसका टुँडालमा कङ्काल र तान्त्रिक आकृति कुँदिएका छन्।

smoke from funeral pyres rising beside the river

lore.title: Where Life Returns to the River
lore.excerpt: Arya Ghat is the principal cremation ghat at Pashupatinath, on the western bank of the Bagmati river beside the main temple. For centuries Hindus have brought their dead here, believing that cremation beside the sacred river at Pashupati, the abode of Shiva, b…

lore.title: Platforms by the Water
lore.excerpt: The ghats consist of stone platforms stepping down to the river, on which funeral pyres are built of wood. Each platform is a raised plinth, sometimes with a small shrine or canopy, and steps allow mourners to carry the body to the water for ritual bathing bef…

lore.title: Fire, Water and Liberation
lore.excerpt: Cremation at Pashupati brings together the elements of fire and water, both sacred in Hindu thought. Fire, Agni, carries the offering of the body to the gods and releases the soul, while the waters of the Bagmati purify the body before cremation and receive th…

lore.title: Rites of Passage
lore.excerpt: Cremations take place at Arya Ghat throughout the day. The family brings the body wrapped in cloth, bathes the feet in the river, places the body on the pyre and performs rituals with the help of priests and ghat attendants. The pyre burns for several hours, a…

lore.title: The River and the Air
lore.excerpt: The greatest environmental challenge at Arya Ghat is the health of the Bagmati river, which has been heavily polluted by urban sewage and waste upstream. Campaigns led by the government and civil society, including a long-running weekly clean-up movement, have…

monuments.audioHook: Below you, on stone platforms beside the river, funeral fires are burning. This is Arya Ghat, the main cremation ghat of Pashupatinath, and for centuries Hindus have believed that being cremated here, in the shadow of Shiva's temple, frees the soul from the cycle of rebirth. Kings were cremated on these steps, includin…
monuments.nepaliSummary: आर्यघाट पशुपतिनाथको मुख्य दाहसंस्कार घाट हो, जहाँ बागमती किनारमा दाहसंस्कार गर्दा मोक्ष प्राप्त हुने विश्वास छ।
monuments.talkingPoint: Explain cremation rites with sensitivity and point out the electric crematorium.

lore.title: Guardian of Pashupati
lore.excerpt: Within the Pashupatinath temple compound stands a shrine to Vasuki, the king of serpents, who is regarded as the guardian of the temple and its treasures. In Hindu mythology Vasuki served as the rope with which the gods and demons churned the cosmic ocean, and…

lore.title: A Shrine Within the Courtyard
lore.excerpt: Vasuki's shrine is one of the many structures within the walled courtyard of Pashupatinath, which is crowded with smaller temples, shrines, lingams and images donated over the centuries. Descriptions indicate a shrine with gilded decoration and serpent imagery…

lore.title: The Serpent King
lore.excerpt: Vasuki is usually depicted as a figure with a human upper body crowned by a multi-headed serpent hood and a serpent's coiled tail below. In the myth of the churning of the ocean, he allowed himself to be used as the churning rope, wrapped around Mount Mandara,…

lore.title: Permission Before Darshan
lore.excerpt: Many devotees visiting Pashupatinath first worship Vasuki, offering flowers, milk and red powder, before proceeding to the main sanctum for darshan of the lingam. This sequence reflects the belief that the serpent guardian controls access to the god. During Na…

lore.title: Documentation Within a Restricted Space
lore.excerpt: Conservation within the Pashupatinath courtyard is managed by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in coordination with the temple's priests, and access for documentation is restricted. Vasuki's shrine, like other structures in the courtyard, is subject to the…

monuments.audioHook: Before Hindu pilgrims enter the inner sanctum of Pashupatinath, many stop first at the shrine of Vasuki, king of the serpents, to ask permission. monuments.nepaliSummary: वासुकिनाथ पशुपतिनाथ मन्दिर परिसरभित्र रहेका नागराज वासुकिको स्थान हो, जसलाई पशुपतिको दर्शनअघि पुजिन्छ।

temple on the east bank of the Bagmati upstream of Pashupatinath
monuments.disambiguationTip: Guhyeshwari's courtyard is upstream on the east bank with a golden canopy held by serpents; the main Pashupatinath temple has two gilded tiered roofs on the west bank.

lore.title: Where the Goddess Fell
lore.excerpt: Guhyeshwari is one of the most sacred Shakti Peeths, the seats of the goddess, in South Asia. According to the myth of Sati, Shiva's wife, she immolated herself after her father insulted Shiva, and the grieving god carried her body across the world. To end his…

lore.title: A Golden Canopy Over a Sacred Pit
lore.excerpt: Guhyeshwari's temple is distinctive: instead of a tiered pagoda roof, the central shrine is covered by a gilded canopy supported by four gilded serpents, whose bodies rise from the corners of the shrine and arch upward to hold the finial. Beneath the canopy, t…

lore.title: The Goddess as Source
lore.excerpt: At Guhyeshwari the goddess is not represented by a sculpted image but by a sacred water source, understood as her womb, the origin of creation. This aniconic form expresses the idea that the feminine power, Shakti, is the source from which all existence arises…

lore.title: Dashain and Tantric Worship
lore.excerpt: Guhyeshwari is a major focus of worship during Dashain, the great festival of the goddess Durga, when large numbers of devotees visit and sacrifices are offered. Throughout the year devotees come to pray for fertility, protection and the fulfilment of wishes, …

lore.title: Caring for a Sacred Spring
lore.excerpt: Guhyeshwari's conservation involves not only its gilded metalwork and buildings but also the sacred water source at its heart, which depends on the health of the local hydrology. Changes in groundwater and the pollution of the Bagmati threaten water sources ac…

monuments.audioHook: Walk upstream along the river to a golden canopy held up by four gilded serpents. This is Guhyeshwari, one of the holiest seats of the goddess in all of South Asia. monuments.talkingPoint: End at the goddess's seat and tell the story of Sati.

lore.excerpt: Kirateshwar Mahadev is a temple to Shiva in his form as Kirata, the hunter, on the eastern slopes of the Pashupati complex above the Bagmati. The name recalls the story, told in the Mahabharata and in the Sanskrit poem Kiratarjuniya, in which Shiva, disguised …

lore.title: A Temple and a Concert Ground
lore.excerpt: Kirateshwar's temple stands on a terrace on the slopes east of the Bagmati, reached by paths and stairs from the riverbank and the Mrigasthali forest. Its architecture is modest, with a shrine housing a Shiva lingam and a Nandi bull facing it, surrounded by sm…

lore.excerpt: In the story of Kirata and Arjuna, the hero Arjuna was performing austerities in the Himalayas to obtain divine weapons for the coming war of the Mahabharata. Shiva appeared as a wild hunter, and when both shot arrows at the same boar, they quarrelled over the…

lore.title: Music Under the Full Moon
lore.excerpt: On full-moon evenings Kirateshwar hosts concerts of Hindustani classical music, a tradition organised for many years by a music ashram connected with the temple. Musicians, from renowned masters to young students, perform ragas on sitar, sarod, flute, tabla an…

lore.title: Sustaining Heritage and Culture
lore.excerpt: Kirateshwar's heritage is both architectural and cultural. The temple and its surroundings lie within the Pashupati monument zone, managed by the Pashupati Area Development Trust, and face the same challenges as other parts of the complex: erosion on the slope…

lore.title: A White Tower in the Forest

lore.title: Sadhus, Shivaratri and Forest Walks
lore.excerpt: Mrigasthali and the Gorakhnath temple come alive during Maha Shivaratri, when thousands of sadhus, including Nath yogis, gather at Pashupati, camping in the forest and around the temples, lighting fires and performing rituals. Pilgrims walk through the plateau…

lore.title: Protecting the Sacred Forest
lore.excerpt: Mrigasthali's forest is an important part of the Pashupati monument zone, providing green space and habitat in a densely urbanised area. Its protection is a priority for the Pashupati Area Development Trust, which manages the area together with conservation of…

monuments.audioHook: Leave the busy riverbank and climb into the forest on the east bank. This is Mrigasthali, the place of deer, where legend says Shiva and Parvati once wandered in the form of deer. lore.excerpt: Each of the fifteen shrines contains a Shiva lingam, the abstract form of the god that represents his infinite creative power. Building a shrine with a lingam in memory of a deceased relative was believed to bring merit to the departed soul and to the family, …

lore.title: A Vantage Point for Devotion

lore.title: A Courtyard for Pilgrims

lore.title: Managing Festival Pressure

lore.excerpt: Panch Deval, meaning 'five temples', is a temple complex on the western bank of the Bagmati at Pashupati, south of the main temple, in which five shrines stand within a walled courtyard. Its date and patrons have not been established in Saalik's sources; it is…
